edits.find:
The adult version — a second discriminator

Upper AND lower respiratory tract involvement together. Pharyngitis plus an interstitial pneumonia is distinctive — typical bacterial pneumonia does not cause pharyngitis. A small serous pleural effusion occurs in ~25% of Mycoplasma, so an effusion is not evidence for pneumococcus; what separates them is everything around it (abrupt onset, rigors, rusty sputum, lobar consolidation, ill appearance).

edits.find:
Purulent or colored discharge does not mean bacterial. Green comes from myeloperoxidase in neutrophils recruited by any inflammation, viral included. Afebrile + well-appearing + 2 days + clear mobile TMs + no exudate + clear lungs → viral URI → supportive care.

The side comes before the color. Unilateral, foul-smelling, purulent discharge in a well, afebrile toddler is a nasal foreign body: the other naris is normal and nothing is systemic. Bacterial sinusitis is bilateral, usually brings fever and cough, and still has to meet a time or severity door below. Clear bilateral discharge with pale, boggy turbinates is allergic; bilateral obstruction with mouth breathing is adenoidal.

edits.find: NBME tests the NAEPP/EPR-3 severity ladder. Intermittent (≤2 days/wk symptoms, ≤2 nights/mo, normal FEV₁, no activity limits) → SABA PRN alone. Mild persistent → add low-dose ICS. Moderate → low-dose ICS+LABA or medium ICS. Severe → high-dose ICS+LABA.
edits.with: NBME tests the NAEPP/EPR-3 severity ladder (National Asthma Education and Prevention Program, Expert Panel Report 3). Intermittent asthma means symptoms ≤2 days/wk, ≤2 nights/mo, normal FEV₁ (forced expiratory volume in 1 second) and no activity limits. Treat it with SABA PRN alone (short-acting beta-agonist, as needed). Mild persistent → add low-dose ICS (inhaled corticosteroid). Moderate → low-dose ICS+LABA (long-acting beta-agonist) or medium ICS. Severe → high-dose ICS+LABA.

edits.find: GINA now states SABA monotherapy is not supported at any step, any severity, any age — even intermittent asthma gets ICS-containing therapy (as-needed ICS-formoterol, or ICS-SABA combination reliever). Rationale: intermittent symptoms do not mean intermittent inflammation. On the exam, play NAEPP; in clinic, GINA. The tell that a question wants NAEPP is an answer ladder running "nothing extra / montelukast / low-dose ICS / ICS+LABA."

edits.find:
Fluid in the interlobar fissures is retained fetal lung fluid — water where it should not be, in a term baby whose lungs are structurally normal — and it appears in no competing diagnosis. Add 88% correcting to 98% on supplemental oxygen, which tells you the problem is alveolar fluid rather than a shunt, and this is transient tachypnea of the newborn.

The mechanism sits in the delivery note. Cesarean without labor is the classic setup, because labor's catecholamine surge is what flips the alveolar epithelium from secreting fluid to absorbing it. Macrosomia at 4200 g rides along as a second risk factor.
